Content covers: the distinction between revenge and grudge-bearing (the axe/sickle parable) and the scholar's own right to forgo his personal honor versus Torah's own honor which he may not; the physical-suffering exemption from this rule reconciled with 'those who are insulted but do not insult'; the lottery's finger-counting mechanics distinguishing healthy from sick participants, and solitary sick individuals who show two fingers but count as one; the ring-finger-permitted/thumb-forbidden anti-fraud rule and its lash-strap ('pakia') penalty, with an extended etymology of pakia via the Temple's worn-priestly-garment wicks; the fatal stabbing on the ramp and Rabbi Tzadok's public proclamation from the portico steps, with the eglah arufah jurisdictional question; the father's declaration over his dying son prioritizing vessel purity over the delayed murder investigation; and the four-cubits/running-in-bloodshed question resolving which mishap (the broken leg or the stabbing) prompted the lottery, closing into the 'ten things about Jerusalem' list continuing onto 23b.
